$frozen: FROZEN. Generated once by backend/tools/generate_sync_vectors.py and asserted byte-for-byte by both backend/tests/sync/ and app/test/sync/. Never regenerated by a test or by CI: regenerating is a protocol change.

aead.aad: the 158 serialized header bytes, exactly — so the suite, the key_epoch and the nonce are all bound with no second binding to keep in step
aead.nonce_source: the header's own nonce field at offset 134, 24 random bytes minted at authoring. Production draws them from a CSPRNG; these vectors pin explicit values, and no seeded-nonce scheme exists in production code.
aead.body_rule: aead_v1 body = XChaCha20-Poly1305 over the *same* framed body plaintext_v1 would carry, so its length is a size class plus the tag. This is the only suite-conditional rule in the codec.
aead.order: verify-then-decrypt on receive: Ed25519 authenticates the author, then the AEAD authenticates the header binding and the confidentiality.
aead.control_ops_are_plaintext_for_ever: An op_class = 2 op under suite 0x01 is refused as encrypted_control_op by both codecs. The server materialises control payloads and holds no key, so an encrypted control op is not a stricter op but one nobody can act on.

keywrap.kdf: HKDF-SHA256(ikm = X25519(esk, kex_pk), salt = empty, info) — the salt being empty means RFC 5869's default of 32 zero bytes. PyNaCl ships no HKDF, so the Python side hand-rolls it (ADR-0037); the Dart side uses package:cryptography's Hkdf, whose `nonce` argument is the RFC's salt. These vectors are what proves the two agree.
keywrap.member_info: b"jeeves/keywrap/v1" || epk 32B || workspace_id 16B || epoch u32 BE || member_id 16B || kex_key_id 8B
keywrap.member_wrap_layout: epk 32B || nonce 24B || XChaCha20-Poly1305(hkdf key, nonce, aad = the info bytes, plaintext = K 32B)
keywrap.escrow_wrap_layout: nonce 24B || XChaCha20-Poly1305(master_wrap_key, nonce, aad = the info bytes, plaintext = K 32B)
keywrap.digest_preimage: SHA-256(b"jeeves/keywrap-digest/v1" || epoch u32 BE || member_wrap_count u32 BE || for each (member_id, kex_key_id, wrap) sorted by (member_id, kex_key_id): member_id 16B || kex_key_id 8B || SHA-256(wrap) 32B || SHA-256(escrow_wrap) 32B)
keywrap.why_not_crypto_box_seal: libsodium's sealed box has no Dart implementation that runs on web, and the vector generator needs a deterministic construction. ADR-0037 records the trade-off.

control.rotate_carries_no_certificate: rotate is the one served type with no cert and no separate signature. Every other type's authority is somebody other than the envelope's author — Root, or a granting Member — so its certificate has to travel independently of who is posting it. A rotate's authority is the author's own live owner Grant, which is the same (role, op_class = 2) rule already applied, so the envelope signature is the only signature there is.
control.rotate_is_single_step: to_epoch must be from_epoch + 1. A rotation that jumped epochs would leave a gap no KeyWrap set is ever minted for, and the epoch floor would then refuse content at an epoch the Workspace never keyed.
control.chain_link: SHA-256 over the predecessor control op's unframed payload bytes — not the envelope, not a re-serialization.
control.zero_chain_link_rule: An all-zero prev_control_hash is legal only on a workspace_genesis. Every other control type carrying one is refused as control_chain_break, even by a receiver whose control state is empty — which is what makes a truncated history always detectable.
control.owner_authority_ceiling: An owner Grant may only be minted with granter "root" and only be revoked with revoker "root". The symmetry is deliberate (ADR-0031): an owner-mints-owner rule would let a compromised device create an attacker-owner cheaply while removing one still cost the passphrase.
control.compaction_exemption_rule: Control ops are never folded into a compaction op, and neither are prune ops: compacting a control op away would delete the evidence a Grant ever existed, and a prune op is itself the attestation that history was removed. #555 enforces this.

escrow.signing_preimage: b"jeeves/escrow/v1" || workspace_id (16 raw bytes) || version (u64 big-endian) || blob
escrow.blob_layout: magic "JVE1" 4B || m_cost_kib u32 || t_cost u32 || parallelism u8 || salt 16B || nonce 24B || XChaCha20-Poly1305(Argon2id(passphrase, salt, params), nonce, aad = the 53 header bytes, root_sk 32B || master_wrap_key 32B)

header_vectors.name: all_zero_header
header_vectors.note: 158 zero bytes — pins the header length itself.

header_vectors.name: distinct_field_probe
header_vectors.note: Every field a distinct byte pattern — pins every offset.

vectors.name: content_set_preference
vectors.note: The smallest real op: one user_preferences write, body in the 256 class.

vectors.name: content_chained_author_seq_2
vectors.note: author_seq 2 with prev_author_hash = SHA-256 of content_set_preference's envelope — pins the per-author chain.

vectors.name: content_tombstone
vectors.note: Deletion is an op, never row absence: empty fields plus tombstone.

vectors.name: content_per_field_hlc
vectors.note: Per-field HLC capability: format now, populated only by compaction ops (#555) re-asserting original clocks.

vectors.name: content_body_size_class_256
vectors.note: Body padded to the 256-byte size class, 32 padding bytes.

vectors.name: content_body_size_class_1024
vectors.note: Body padded to the 1024-byte size class, 32 padding bytes.

vectors.name: content_body_size_class_4096
vectors.note: Body padded to the 4096-byte size class, 32 padding bytes.

vectors.name: content_body_size_class_16384
vectors.note: Body padded to the 16384-byte size class, 32 padding bytes.

vectors.name: content_body_oversize_32768
vectors.note: Above the largest size class a body rounds up to the next 16 KiB multiple, with no hard cap.

negative_vectors.name: unknown_suite
negative_vectors.note: Suite 0x7F is not a value the protocol names. Fail closed (F21).

negative_vectors.name: encrypted_control_op
negative_vectors.note: A validly signed, validly sealed member_register under suite 0x01. Refused by both codecs: control ops are plaintext_v1 for ever, because the server materialises their payloads and holds no key. Both halves of the pair are served and the pair is forbidden, which is why this is not expressible as a served-set membership test.

negative_vectors.name: unimplemented_op_class_compaction
negative_vectors.note: op_class 4 is a named class this slice does not implement. It quarantines on the same surface as an unknown value; #555 turns this into a positive vector.

negative_vectors.name: truncated_header
negative_vectors.note: One byte short of the 158-byte header.

negative_vectors.name: truncated_envelope_no_body
negative_vectors.note: Exactly the 222-byte overhead: no body at all.

negative_vectors.name: bad_signature
negative_vectors.note: Last signature byte flipped; header and body untouched.

negative_vectors.name: non_zero_padding
negative_vectors.note: The non-zero byte sits at offset 196 = 4 + payload_len, the *first* padding position, so an off-by-one in the padding scan cannot pass this vector. Signed over the tampered body, so only the padding rule fires.

negative_vectors.name: invalid_padded_length
negative_vectors.note: 300-byte body: neither a size class nor a 16384-byte multiple.

negative_vectors.name: payload_overruns_body
negative_vectors.note: payload_len is the whole body length, so 4 + payload_len > body_len. The frame must be rejected before any byte of it is read as a payload.

negative_vectors.name: uppercase_member_id_hex
negative_vectors.note: HLC member ids are exactly 32 lowercase hex characters. The tie-break is a lexicographic string compare, so an uppercase id would order differently — codecs reject rather than normalise.

negative_vectors.name: malformed_entity_id
negative_vectors.note: The right 32 hex digits, dashes removed.  Python's `uuid.UUID` accepts this spelling and the Dart codec's `uuidToBytes` does not, so it is exactly the shape the two codecs used to disagree about.  Both now require the canonical lowercase 8-4-4-4-12 form and reject the rest rather than normalising, as they do for an HLC member id.

negative_vectors.name: workspace_mismatch
negative_vectors.note: Header workspace disagrees with the stream it arrived in: a server-integrity event, not a filtered row (F6). The plaintext-era analogue of 'AEAD failure is an alarm'.

control_vectors.name: workspace_genesis
control_vectors.note: The Workspace comes into being: author_seq 1, an all-zero prev_control_hash — the only op that may carry one — and a Root signature under jeeves/workspace-genesis/v1. The certificate embeds the founding Device's registration, because the envelope's author key is unknowable before the certificate parses and there is no earlier op to learn it from (ADR-0031). root_pk sits inside the signed bytes so every later verifier can cross-check the Root it pinned.

control_vectors.name: grant_founder_owner
control_vectors.note: Roles are one materialisation path: no implied grants, genesis included. The founder is an owner because Root said so in a separate signed fact, and revoking it later invalidates nothing (F14d). An owner role may only be minted with granter "root" — the mint half of the ceiling ADR-0031 records.

control_vectors.name: member_register_second_device
control_vectors.note: The Nth Device's registration: its own author_seq 1, chained to the control head it observed by SHA-256 over that op's *payload bytes*, so the link is computable from the unencrypted payload alone and survives any future envelope-level re-framing. A zero link here would be refused even by an empty receiver — that is genesis-only.

control_vectors.name: grant_second_device_owner
control_vectors.note: Devices are owners because the User acts through them, and the corollary is deliberate: revoking a Device takes the passphrase, because only Root can revoke an owner Grant.

control_vectors.name: grant_service_suggester_owner_signed
control_vectors.note: An owning Device granting a *non-owner* role, signed with its own key rather than Root's: the envelope author, the payload's granter and the certificate's granter are all the same member, because authority does not travel by courier. A Grant carries no key material, which is why the grantee here needs no keypair at all.

control_vectors.name: revoke_service_suggester
control_vectors.note: Revocation is grant-granular: the certificate names one grant_id, never a member (F19). Revoking the granter would not cascade — a fact valid at the position it was signed at stands, because nothing re-evaluates it (F14c).

control_vectors.name: rotate_to_epoch_1
control_vectors.note: Turning encryption on *is* a rotation — no separate switch, no second machine. from_epoch 0 to_epoch 1, so epoch 0 is never keyed and this Workspace's pre-turn-on plaintext history stays readable for ever. The one control type with no certificate and no separate signature: its authority is the author's own live owner Grant, so the envelope signature is the only signature there is. keywrap_digest commits to the whole wrap set *before* any wrap is uploaded, which is what stops the server curating who can read the new epoch — it matches keywrap_digest_two_members_epoch_1 exactly.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_bad_root_signature
negative_control_vectors.note: Last byte of the Root signature flipped; the envelope itself is validly signed by the device. Without Root behind it a certificate is a claim, not a registration.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_unsupported_type
negative_control_vectors.note: A control type this build does not serve. Rotating a *Member's* own signing or KEX key is a different thing from rotating the Workspace content key, which `rotate` now does: every type outside the five served ones stays fail-closed, and the payload beyond the two self-identifying fields is not even parsed.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_malformed_payload
negative_control_vectors.note: A served type with an empty certificate and an empty signature: the self-identifying fields parse and nothing else does.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_no_type_field
negative_control_vectors.note: No `type` field and a short chain hash. Every control payload must be self-identifying: a chain link points at bare payload bytes, so nothing outside the payload can say what it is.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_member_register_with_zero_chain_link
negative_control_vectors.note: An all-zero prev_control_hash is **genesis-only** (ADR-0031). Refused even by a receiver whose control state is empty, which is what makes a truncated history always detectable: treating a zero link as 'fresh chain' is exactly the claim a server serving a truncated log makes.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_genesis_with_a_non_zero_chain_link
negative_control_vectors.note: The mirror rule: genesis is the Workspace's *first* control op, so it must carry the zero link and nothing else. A genesis naming a predecessor is a second genesis wearing a chain.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_grant_bad_granter_signature
negative_control_vectors.note: Last byte of the granter's signature flipped. Authority rides in the signed certificate bytes, so an unsigned Grant is a request rather than a fact.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_revoke_bad_revoker_signature
negative_control_vectors.note: The same rule on the unmaking side, under its own domain: a signature made over a Grant must never verify over a Revoke.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_grant_unknown_role
negative_control_vectors.note: A role outside owner/participant/compactor/suggester, validly Root-signed. It still fails closed: a role a verifier cannot interpret must never be read as a permissive default.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_grant_owner_role_minted_by_a_member
negative_control_vectors.note: The mint half of the owner ceiling, and a pure document invariant: `role: owner` under any granter but Root is refused at decode, wherever the bytes are held. ADR-0031 records why the ceiling is symmetric with revocation — an owner-mints-owner rule would let a compromised device create an attacker-owner cheaply while removing one still cost the passphrase, and that asymmetry favours the attacker.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_grant_certificate_missing_member_id
negative_control_vectors.note: A Root-signed Grant with no grantee. A valid signature over an incomplete document authenticates the bytes and says nothing about their meaning, so the field rules run anyway.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_certificate_member_mismatch
negative_control_vectors.note: One device's genuinely Root-signed registration wrapped around another device's envelope. A certificate is public the moment it is in the log, so the binding step asks who it is *about*: the member identity is compared before the envelope is verified under the certificate's key, and this refuses as the member mismatch rather than as the signature failure that would follow. `cert_member_mismatch` names the certificate's subject as the field that disagreed — the same code the server returns.

negative_control_vectors.name: control_certificate_key_mismatch
negative_control_vectors.note: The certificate is about this author and its key really did sign this envelope — the header just names a different device's key id. Envelope verification therefore *passes*, and the derived key-id comparison after it is what fires. `cert_key_mismatch` means the header names a key the certificate does not carry, which is a different attack from a certificate about somebody else and remediated differently.

aead_vectors.name: aead_content_set_preference
aead_vectors.note: The plaintext_v1 vector content_set_preference, sealed. Same framed body, same 256-byte size class inside; the wire body is that plus a 16-byte tag. AAD is the 158 header bytes exactly.

aead_vectors.name: aead_content_at_epoch_2
aead_vectors.note: A second epoch under a different key. key_epoch is inside the AAD, so a body sealed at one epoch cannot be replayed as another's even if the keys were somehow the same.

aead_vectors.name: aead_content_body_size_class_1024
aead_vectors.note: Pad-then-encrypt at a larger class, chained at author_seq 2: the padding rules run on the decrypted plaintext through the same code path plaintext_v1 uses.

negative_aead_vectors.name: aead_tampered_ciphertext
negative_aead_vectors.note: One ciphertext byte flipped and the envelope re-signed, so the signature verifies and the AEAD is what refuses it. Verify-then-decrypt is the receive order; this is the second gate firing.

negative_aead_vectors.name: aead_tampered_header_key_epoch
negative_aead_vectors.note: key_epoch changed and the envelope re-signed. The AAD is the literal header, so the body no longer authenticates: aead_failure, not bad_signature. A server cannot re-label an op's epoch.

negative_aead_vectors.name: aead_wrong_epoch_key
negative_aead_vectors.note: The genuine epoch-1 envelope, offered with the epoch-2 key. Refused as aead_failure — a key we hold that does not open the bytes is an accusation, distinct from missing_epoch_key which is a delivery gap.

negative_aead_vectors.name: aead_body_is_a_bare_size_class
negative_aead_vectors.note: A 0x01 body of exactly 256 bytes. Legal for plaintext_v1 and illegal here: an aead_v1 body is a size class plus the 16-byte tag. The one suite-conditional rule in the codec.

keywrap_vectors.name: keywrap_device_a_epoch_1
keywrap_vectors.note: epk || nonce || XChaCha20-Poly1305 over the 32-byte epoch key. The HKDF info and the AEAD AAD are the same bytes, and epk is inside them (HPKE discipline), so nothing about the wrap can be re-pointed at another member, epoch, Workspace or key.

keywrap_vectors.name: keywrap_device_b_epoch_1
keywrap_vectors.note: epk || nonce || XChaCha20-Poly1305 over the 32-byte epoch key. The HKDF info and the AEAD AAD are the same bytes, and epk is inside them (HPKE discipline), so nothing about the wrap can be re-pointed at another member, epoch, Workspace or key.

keywrap_vectors.name: epoch_key_escrow_wrap_epoch_1
keywrap_vectors.note: The same epoch key under the escrowed master_wrap_key. This is what makes a fresh device's bootstrap work with no live second device: passphrase -> master_wrap_key -> every historical epoch key.

keywrap_vectors.name: keywrap_digest_two_members_epoch_1
keywrap_vectors.note: The commitment a rotate op carries. Entries are sorted by (member_id, kex_key_id) so the digest is a property of the set and not of an upload order the server could shuffle, and the escrow wrap is inside it so the server can neither add nor omit any wrap.

keywrap_vectors.name: keywrap_replayed_into_another_member_slot
keywrap_vectors.note: device_a's genuine wrap, unwrapped as if it were device_b's. member_id and kex_key_id are inside the info, so the derived key differs and the AEAD refuses: aead_failure. An honest-but-confused server cannot misroute a wrap.

keywrap_vectors.name: keywrap_replayed_into_another_epoch
keywrap_vectors.note: device_b's genuine epoch-1 wrap, unwrapped as if it were epoch 2. The epoch is inside the info, so a server cannot hand yesterday's key over as today's.

escrow_vectors.name: escrow_v1_signature_version_1
escrow_vectors.note: The first write. workspace_id sits inside the signed bytes, so a blob signed for one Workspace can never be replayed into another.

escrow_vectors.name: escrow_v1_signature_version_2
escrow_vectors.note: A passphrase change re-wraps at v+1. The version is inside the preimage too, so a signature does not transfer between versions.

member_challenge_vectors.name: auth_challenge_v1
member_challenge_vectors.note: The member id is inside the signed bytes, so a captured signature cannot be replayed into another member's slot.
